name: First American Bankshares

summary.text: First American Bankshares was the Washington, D.C. bank holding company formed when Financial General Bankshares was acquired in 1981-82 by Credit and Commerce American Holdings (CCAH), a group of Gulf investors led by Kamal Adham, with Clark Clifford as chairman and Robert Altman as president. The Federal Reserve approved the acquisition in 1981 on representations that BCCI was not involved; in July 1991 the Board found that BCCI had in fact owned CCAH in violation of the Bank Holding Company Act and had concealed its control at the time of the application. The Senate Foreign Relations Committee's 1992 report found the Fed had substantial circumstantial evidence of BCCI's role at the time and that the CIA made extensive use of First American's accounts. Under a court-supervised order the Washington-area banks were sold to First Union in 1993 for $453 million. The BCCI, Clifford, Adham and Altman files on this site hold the individuals' records; this file holds the bank's.

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee's December 1992 report concluded that when the Federal Reserve approved CCAH's takeover of Financial General Bankshares in 1981 it had substantial circumstantial evidence that BCCI was behind the purchase, but chose not to act on it because of specific representations from CCAH's shareholders and lawyers that BCCI was not involved, representations the report says were untrue and without which the Fed would not have approved the application.
facts.quote: The Fed chose not to act on that evidence because of the specific representations from CCAH's shareholders and lawyers that BCCI was not involved.

facts.claim: After the takeover, Financial General Bankshares renamed its banks First American and its holding company First American Corporation; Kamal Adham was the lead investor in the CCAH group, officially on his own behalf but, the Senate report found, acting as a nominee for BCCI.
facts.quote: FGB formally changed the name of its banks to First American, and its holding company to First American Corporation.

facts.claim: On July 29, 1991 the Federal Reserve Board announced enforcement proceedings finding that BCCI owned Credit and Commerce American Holdings, First American's parent, in violation of the Bank Holding Company Act and had concealed its intended ownership and control of CCAH at the time of the 1980 application to acquire First American; the Board assessed a $200 million civil penalty against BCCI.
facts.quote: BCCI owned CCAH in violation of the Bank Holding Company Act, and BCCI concealed its intended ownership and control of CCAH at the time of CCAH's 1980 application to acquire First American.

facts.claim: The Senate report records that in October 1991 Acting CIA Director Richard Kerr acknowledged that the CIA had made extensive use of First American for a variety of purposes including ordinary banking and savings accounts, and that the agency had given the Treasury information about BCCI's secret ownership of First American by 1985.
facts.quote: the CIA had made extensive use of First American

facts.claim: Under BCCI's January 1992 plea agreement, about $100 million of forfeited funds was earmarked to support First American Bankshares, BCCI's main American subsidiary.
facts.quote: approximately $100 million of the forfeited funds would be used to support BCCI's main American subsidiary, First American Bankshares Inc.

sources.publisher: UPI
sources.title: Judge accepts BCCI plea

facts.claim: On February 26, 1993 First Union Corp. of Charlotte announced it would buy First American's Washington-area banks for $453 million; First American was under a federal court order to be sold by June 23, 1993 because of its past illegal ownership by BCCI, with the sale subject to regulators and to court-appointed trustee Harry W. Albright Jr.
facts.quote: First Union Corp. of Charlotte, N.C., announced it will buy First American Bancorp's Washington area banks for $453 million

openQuestions: The Fed's approval date differs by source (August 25, 1981 per the House Banking report; April 1982 per a secondary site); the 1981 date is used.
The Fed 1991 PDF and UPI 1992 URLs are carried from bcci.json and were not re-opened in this session; the FAS chapters and the Washington Post 1993 article were returned by search.
